name: ssd-bench-conv-planning
notes: Multi-turn conversation: sprint planning for an observability feature. system+user+assistant+user chain totalling ~640 tokens.

messages.content: You are a technical program manager helping a small engineering team plan a sprint. You help break down large features into well-scoped, independently deployable tasks. You ask clarifying questions, identify dependencies, and flag risks. Each task you propose has: a title, a one-sentence scope statement, an estimated complexity (S/M/L where S=half-day, M=1 day, L=2-3 days), explicit input and output artifacts, and the dependency chain.

We want to add a comprehensive observability layer to our Rust-based LLM inference server. The goal is: within 10 seconds of any inference request completing, we can query a dashboard and see for that request: (1) total latency breakdown by phase — time waiting in queue, prefill time, decode time, first-token latency; (2) prompt-cache tier stats — whether the request was a RAM hit, SSD hit, or full miss; (3) KV-cache memory footprint at the time of the request; (4) SSD spill and hydrate events triggered by the request; (5) token-level decode speed (tokens per second for that specific request, not a rolling average). We have the following existing infrastructure: a Prometheus /metrics endpoint that currently only exposes aggregate counters, a SQLite metrics database (runs.db) where we record per-run observations, an async drainer task that batches writes to SQLite, and a tracing subscriber that writes structured JSON events to per-run JSONL files. We do not have Grafana set up yet. Sprint is two weeks, team of three engineers.

Here is my proposed task breakdown. I am organizing it into four tracks that can be parallelized across three engineers after the first dependency.

Track 0 (prerequisite, one task):

T0: Per-request correlation ID (S)
Scope: Generate a UUID per inference request at HTTP ingestion and thread it through all async tasks, tracing spans, and SQLite writes as a request_id field.
Input: Existing request handler. Output: request_id present in all tracing events and available to downstream tasks.
Dependency: None. Must complete before T1–T7.

Track A — Prometheus per-request histograms (Engineer 1, week 1):

T1: Latency phase histograms (M)
Scope: Add four Prometheus histograms (queue_wait_us, prefill_us, decode_us, ttft_us) instrumented at the appropriate code sites. Expose via /metrics.
Input: T0 (request_id), existing /metrics handler. Output: Four new histograms queryable in Prometheus.
Dependency: T0.

T2: Cache tier result counter (S)
Scope: Add a prompt_cache_result{tier=ram|ssd|miss} counter incremented per request. Wire to the existing CacheStats path.
Input: Existing CacheStats struct. Output: Counter visible in /metrics.
Dependency: T0.

T3: Per-request decode TPS histogram (S)
Scope: Record decode elapsed and token count per request; emit a decode_tps Prometheus histogram and a summary with request_id label in the response JSON (ssd_hits already done, extend to include decode_tps_this_request).
Input: Existing response serializer. Output: Histogram + field in JSON response.
Dependency: T1.

Track B — SQLite per-request event rows (Engineer 2, week 1):

T4: Schema migration for per-request events (S)
Scope: Add migration 003_requests.sql: a requests table with columns request_id, model_id, ts_utc, queue_wait_us, prefill_us, decode_us, ttft_us, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, cache_tier, kv_bytes, ssd_spill_count, ssd_hydrate_count.
Input: Existing migration runner. Output: Schema deployed on next server start.
Dependency: T0.

T5: Drainer writes request row (M)
Scope: Extend the existing DrainerHandle to accept a new RequestRecord event variant. The async drainer consumer inserts one row per completed request using spawn_blocking.
Input: T4 schema, T0 request_id. Output: One row per request in the requests table within 10 s of completion.
Dependency: T4.

Track C — SSD event correlation (Engineer 3, week 1):

T6: Tag SSD spill/hydrate events with request_id (M)
Scope: Thread request_id through the SSD spiller and hydrator call sites. Update the events table INSERT to include a request_id column (migration 003 or 004). Count spill/hydrate events per request and pass the counts to the DrainerHandle RequestRecord.
Input: T4, existing spill/hydrate event recording. Output: events rows tagged with request_id; counts available for T5.
Dependency: T4, T5.

Week 2 (all three engineers):

T7: Grafana dashboard (L)
Scope: Stand up Grafana (Docker Compose), configure Prometheus datasource, create dashboard with six panels: latency breakdown stacked bar, cache tier pie chart, decode TPS heatmap, SSD bytes used gauge, eviction rate counter, KV memory trend line.
Input: T1–T3 Prometheus metrics, T5–T6 SQLite data via sqlite_exporter or direct Prometheus remote-write. Output: Dashboard accessible at localhost:3000.
Dependency: T1, T2, T3.

T8: Integration test (M)
Scope: Add a test that starts the server, sends 10 requests, queries /metrics and runs.db, asserts all five observable dimensions are populated within 10 s.
Input: T5, T6, T7. Output: Passing test in CI.
Dependency: T5, T6.

Risks: T7 is the largest unknown — Grafana setup often takes longer than estimated. If T7 slips, the sprint goal can still be met using sqlite3 CLI queries as a temporary dashboard (document the queries). T6 requires touching the hot decode path — allocate time for performance regression testing.

This is very useful. I have two follow-up questions. First, for T6 you mention threading request_id through the SSD spiller and hydrator — but our spiller runs in a background drain thread that is decoupled from the request lifecycle by a channel. The spill is triggered when a prompt-cache slot is evicted, which may happen many requests after the original prefill that filled that slot. How should we correlate a spill event to the original request that produced the cached block? Is it even useful to try, or should we just record spills as namespace-level events with no request-id? Second, for T8, what is the right assertion strategy for the '10 seconds' liveness guarantee — should we poll the database in a loop with a timeout, use a tokio::time::timeout around a query future, or set up a test-specific Prometheus scrape?
